I'm 64 years old and I've farmed these flat fields in Quzhou County for over forty years. I have about 5 mu of good alluvial soil on the North China Plain, and I rely on my well for irrigation. At my age, I don't take risks with new crops or fancy experiments — I stick to the double-cropping system that has always put food on my table and money in my pocket. This year, just like every year, I'll plant winter wheat and summer maize on my full 5 mu. 

For the wheat, I'll sow an improved variety like *shimai* or *liangxing* around early October. Before sowing, I'll rotary till the land to break up the stubble and level the field. I'll put down basal compound fertilizer — the 18-22-5 blend we get locally, about 100 jin per mu — and in spring I'll topdress with ammonium bicarbonate when the wheat greens up. I irrigate three times: a winter irrigation to protect against freezing, and two more in spring when the dry winds blow through. I'll spray for aphids and fusarium a couple of times and use herbicide once. If the weather holds, I should get around 500 kg per mu.

Come early June, as soon as the wheat is off the thresher, I'll plant maize directly into the stubble with no-tillage — saves time, fuel, and my back. I'll buy hybrid seed from the supply shop, probably something like Nongda372 or NK815. At planting, I'll spread compound fertilizer, the 28-6-6 type, about 90 jin per mu. Maize doesn't need as much water as wheat — twice with border irrigation is usually enough. I'll spray insecticide and herbicide, maybe three applications total. With good hybrid seed, I expect about 600 kg per mu.

I thought about planting cotton or vegetables, but at my age the labor is too heavy and the prices jump around. Wheat and maize have steady markets — the grain collection station and local feed traders always buy — and I can keep some for my own flour and chicken feed. That's my plan.
